evidence.claim: From Cleopatra Hill’s mining town to the Verde Valley’s old downtowns
evidence.quote: Founded in the late 19th century on Cleopatra Hill overlooking the Verde Valley

evidence.claim: the Verde Valley’s old downtowns
evidence.quote: Historic US 89A, runs through the old downtown areas of both Clarkdale and Cottonwood.

evidence.claim: This drive descends from Jerome toward the Verde Valley, then follows Historic 89A through the old downtowns of Clarkdale and Cottonwood.
evidence.quote: During its descent, SR 89A enters the town of Jerome.

evidence.claim: This drive descends from Jerome toward the Verde Valley
evidence.quote: Upon exiting Jerome, SR 89A heads northeast through the Verde Valley.

evidence.claim: In Jerome, buildings line winding roads on the steep mountainside.
evidence.quote: with buildings perched along the winding roads of the steeply sloped mountainside.

evidence.claim: The Arizona Department of Transportation designated the Jerome-Clarkdale-Cottonwood Historic Road in 1992; the historic route is about 10 miles long.
evidence.quote: The historic route was designated on May 13, 1992, by ADOT and is about 10 miles long.

evidence.claim: United Verde built wagon roads from Jerome to Prescott, the Verde Valley and the railway depot at Ash Fork. Expensive wagon transport and a sharp copper-price fall helped bring operations to a halt in 1884.
evidence.quote: United Verde built a small smelter at Jerome and constructed wagon roads from it to Prescott, the Verde Valley, and the Atlantic and Pacific Railroad depot at Ash Fork. However, transport by wagon was expensive, and in late 1884 after the price of copper had fallen by 50%, the company ceased all operations at the site.

evidence.claim: United Verde built wagon roads
evidence.quote: United Verde built a small smelter at Jerome and constructed wagon roads

evidence.claim: The larger highway first entered the state system in 1927 as State Route 79, when only the Prescott-to-Clarkdale portion had been built.
evidence.quote: The routing of SR 89A was first defined as a state highway in 1927 as SR 79 by the Arizona Department of Transportation (ADOT). At the time, only the portion from Prescott to Clarkdale was built

evidence.claim: Pavement reached the Jerome-to-Cottonwood section before the entire highway was paved in 1938.
evidence.quote: The southern end of the highway near Prescott and the section between Jerome and Cottonwood had been paved by this time. By 1938, the entire route had been paved.

evidence.claim: The highway became U.S. 89A in 1941 and State Route 89A in 1993.
evidence.quote: By 1941, the highway was redesignated from SR 79 to US 89A.

evidence.claim: The highway became U.S. 89A in 1941 and State Route 89A in 1993.
evidence.quote: The route was redesignated from US 89A to SR 89A in 1993.

evidence.claim: The historic route now takes in the downtown streets while the state highway follows a different course through Clarkdale and Cottonwood.
evidence.quote: Historic US 89A, runs through the old downtown areas of both Clarkdale and Cottonwood.

evidence.claim: the state highway follows a different course through Clarkdale and Cottonwood
evidence.quote: After SR 89A and Historic US 89A enter the town of Clarkdale, SR 89A turns southeast at a roundabout with Clarkdale Parkway.

evidence.claim: Begin with Jerome on Cleopatra Hill, above the valley communities of Clarkdale and Cottonwood.
evidence.quote: East of Jerome at the base of the hills are the Verde Valley and the communities of Clarkdale and Cottonwood

evidence.claim: From the roundabout at Clarkdale Parkway, the historic route runs north, then follows Main Street and Broadway through Clarkdale.
evidence.quote: From the present day traffic circle between SR 89A and Clarkdale Parkway, Historic 89A continues north along Clarkdale Parkway, turning right at Main Street in Clarkdale, and then right again at Broadway.

evidence.claim: It passes Tuzigoot National Monument before becoming Cottonwood’s Main Street and meeting Cottonwood Street.
evidence.quote: It continues past Tuzigoot National Monument, becoming Main Street in Cottonwood, and providing access to Dead Horse Ranch State Park. The route intersects Cottonwood Street, where the bypass route now intersects Main Street.

evidence.claim: Jerome’s buildings follow winding streets across a steep mountainside, the setting of a copper town that outlived its mines.
evidence.quote: The community retains much of the look and feel of an early 20th-century mining town, with buildings perched along the winding roads of the steeply sloped mountainside.

evidence.claim: Mining ended in 1953, and the population fell below 100.
evidence.quote: Mining continued at a reduced level in the Verde District until 1953, when Phelps Dodge shut down the United Verde Mine and related operations. Jerome's population subsequently fell below 100.

evidence.claim: Residents organized the Jerome Historical Society that year and opened a museum and gift shop as they turned to tourism.
evidence.quote: They organized the Jerome Historical Society in 1953 and opened a museum and gift shop.

evidence.claim: as they turned to tourism
evidence.quote: its remaining residents turned to tourism and retail sales.

evidence.claim: In 1956, the society completed negotiations with Phelps Dodge to prevent further demolition in the town’s main section.
evidence.quote: In 1956 the society completed negotiations with Phelps Dodge assuring that no more buildings would be torn down in the main part of Jerome.

evidence.claim: Formerly vacant buildings now house gift, antique and craft shops, and the former high school complex contains artists’ galleries.
evidence.quote: Formerly vacant buildings house boutiques and gift, antique, and craft shops;

evidence.claim: the former high school complex contains artists’ galleries
evidence.quote: The former Jerome High School complex is home in the 21st century to many artists' galleries.

evidence.claim: Society plaques identify historic properties among the surviving buildings.
evidence.quote: Structures identified as historical by the Jerome Historical Society Plaque Project have a mounted plaque, placed by the society.

evidence.claim: Clarkdale was planned around the work of processing Jerome’s copper ore.
evidence.quote: Clarkdale was founded in 1912 as a company smelter town by William A. Clark, for his copper mine in nearby Jerome.

evidence.claim: William A. Clark founded the company town in 1912, with services that included electricity, telephones, sewers and spring water.
evidence.quote: including telephone, telegraph, electrical, sewer and spring water services

evidence.claim: That planning also enforced divisions: engineers and executives lived in Upper Clarkdale, while workers occupied Lower Clarkdale.
evidence.quote: Upper Clarkdale was designated for engineers and executives, while Lower Clarkdale was for the "working class."

evidence.claim: Mexican and Mexican-American laborers were restricted to Patio Town, with a separate pool and park.
evidence.quote: Mexican and Mexican-American laborers were restricted to living in Patio Town (see neighborhoods), with a separate swimming pool and park

evidence.claim: The mine and smelter closed in 1953. Clarkdale incorporated four years later, and a cement plant followed in 1959.
evidence.quote: The mine and smelter closed in 1953, and Clarkdale entered hard times. Clarkdale was bought and sold by several different companies. In 1957, Clarkdale was incorporated as a town. The 1959 construction of the Phoenix Cement Company

evidence.claim: The original town site is on the National Register, and the Clark Memorial Clubhouse and Memorial Library remain in use.
evidence.quote: The town center and business district were built in Spanish Colonial style, and feature the Clark Memorial Clubhouse and Memorial Library, both still in use.

evidence.claim: The original town site is on the National Register
evidence.quote: The entire original town site is also on the National Register as the Clarkdale Historic District.

evidence.claim: Tuzigoot’s 110 rooms occupy a ridge above the Verde River floodplain.
evidence.quote: preserves a 2- to 3-story pueblo ruin on the summit of a limestone and sandstone ridge just east of Clarkdale, Arizona, 120 feet (37 m) above the Verde River floodplain.

evidence.claim: 110 rooms
evidence.quote: The pueblo has 110 rooms.

evidence.claim: The Sinagua built the pueblo above farmland, with the Verde River and Black Hills providing resources.
evidence.quote: Tuzigoot was built on a low hilltop in the Verde Valley. The Verde River and Black Hills provided a variety of resource areas for the Sinagua.

evidence.claim: above farmland
evidence.quote: Tuzigoot Pueblo sits on a hilltop above an area perfect for farming.

evidence.claim: Few doorways pierce the rooms; residents used ladders through roof openings.
evidence.quote: The ruins at Tuzigoot incorporate very few doors; instead, the inhabitants used ladders accessed by trapdoor type openings in the roofs to enter each room.

evidence.claim: Excavation took place from 1933 to 1935, followed by work to prepare the ruins for public display.
evidence.quote: Tuzigoot was excavated from 1933 to 1935 by Louis Caywood and Edward Spicer of the University of Arizona

evidence.claim: followed by work to prepare the ruins for public display
evidence.quote: In 1935–1936, with additional federal funding, the ruins were prepared for public display

evidence.claim: The National Park Service identifies a room rebuilt in the 1930s whose roof was not part of its original form.
evidence.quote: Rebuilt in the 1930s, this room at Tuzigoot would not originally have had a roof.

evidence.claim: The museum displays artifacts found at the site, while Tavasci Marsh provides perennial wetlands nearby.
evidence.quote: Explore the Museum Learn about artifacts found on-site to catch a glimpse of life in ancient Arizona Tavasci Marsh Explore the perennial wetlands of the Tavasci marsh, home to a unique variety of wildlife and plant life.

evidence.claim: Look at the stone rooms extending along the ridge’s spine.
evidence.quote: The Tuzigoot Site is an elongated complex of stone masonry rooms that were built along the spine of a natural outcrop in the Verde Valley.
